selected_passages.title: sources/Apple_defends_Google_Search_deal_in_court_There_wasn_t_a_valid_alternative
selected_passages.text:
- Eddy Cue testified that there was no valid alternative to Google Search for Apple devices at the time of the deal.
- The Information Services Agreement (ISA) makes Google the default search engine on Apple products in exchange for billions in payments.
- Apple believes in protecting user privacy but also maintains a strong partnership with Google, creating a central tension in the trial.
- Cue argued that showing users alternative search engines during setup would degrade the user experience and slow down device onboarding.
- The Justice Department questions whether Apple's choice of Google is based on product quality or financial incentives.

selected_passages.text: In the landmark US v. Google antitrust trial, Apple witness Eddy Cue testified that Google Search was the only viable alternative for Apple devices, despite the Justice Department's focus on the lucrative Information Services Agreement (ISA). Cue argued that Apple prioritizes user experience and privacy, claiming Google offers the best product and that switching engines is seamless, while acknowledging Apple's belief in Google's privacy policies even as they criticize Google's own practices.
selected_passages.context_block:
[sources/Apple_defends_Google_Search_deal_in_court_There_wasn_t_a_valid_alternative]
In the landmark US v. Google antitrust trial, Apple witness Eddy Cue testified that Google Search was the only viable alternative for Apple devices, despite the Justice Department's focus on the lucrative Information Services Agreement (ISA). Cue argued that Apple prioritizes user experience and privacy, claiming Google offers the best product and that switching engines is seamless, while acknowledging Apple's belief in Google's privacy policies even as they criticize Google's own practices.

selected_passages.title: sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case
selected_passages.text:
- Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to become the default search engine on various platforms.
- The Department of Justice claims Google's dominance hinders competitors by blocking access to advertising and search data.
- Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users as part of its deal with Apple.
- Pichai admitted attempting to get Google preinstalled on iPhones in 2018, which Apple declined.
- The trial highlights Google's hypocrisy regarding default search engine settings compared to its past actions against Microsoft.
